children.text: Two traders look at the same MCX gold quote screen. One buys the near-month contract outright, betting gold prices will rise. The other buys the near-month contract and simultaneously sells a far-month contract on the very same gold, betting on nothing about gold's direction at all, only on how the gap between the two contracts will change. If gold rallies 5% tomorrow, the first trader profits handsomely and the second barely notices, because both of their contracts moved together and the gap between them barely budged. This second trade is a spread, and it is a genuinely different way to use futures than anything covered so far in this course.

body.text: A spread trade profits from the relationship, the price difference, between two contracts rather than from the absolute direction of either one. That usually means lower risk and lower potential reward than an outright position, and often lower margin, since the two legs largely offset each other against a broad market move.

children.text: Calendar Spreads: Trading Near-Month vs Far-Month

markDefs.definition: A spread position built entirely within one commodity, buying one contract month and selling a different contract month of the same underlying.

children.text: Chapter 2 showed that in a contango market, a farther-dated contract normally trades above a nearer one, by roughly the cost of financing and storage. A

trades exactly that gap, rather than the direction of the underlying price. Recall the earlier illustrative example: gold spot-equivalent at ₹60,000 per 10 grams, with the fair 3-month futures price worked out to ₹61,125, a spread of ₹1,125.

body.caption: Two ways to trade the same gold calendar spread

cells: Financing/storage costs will rise, or the spread will widen
Buy the far-month contract, sell the near-month contract
The gap grows beyond ₹1,125, regardless of which direction gold itself moves
The spread looks too wide and should narrow
Sell the far-month contract, buy the near-month contract
The gap shrinks below ₹1,125, regardless of which direction gold itself moves

body.label: A common (but not universal) margin benefit
body.value: Spread positions can require less margin than two separate outright positions
body.context: Because a calendar spread's two legs largely cancel out a broad market move, exchanges and brokers sometimes offer reduced margin on qualifying spread positions. Which specific contracts qualify changes over time, so always confirm current margin treatment with your broker before assuming a discount applies.

body.title: What does a calendar spread actually bet on?
body.question: A trader buys the far-month MCX Silver contract and sells the near-month MCX Silver contract. What outcome does this position profit from?
options: Silver's overall price rising, regardless of the spread
Silver's overall price falling, regardless of the spread
The gap between the far-month and near-month prices widening
The gap between the far-month and near-month prices staying exactly zero
body.explanation: Buying the far-month leg and selling the near-month leg profits if the far-month price rises relative to the near-month price, that is, if the spread widens. Since both legs are in the same commodity, a broad move in silver's overall price affects both legs similarly and mostly cancels out.

markDefs.definition: A spread position built across two different but related commodities, rather than two contract months of the same one.

children.text: trades the relationship between two related commodities instead of two months of one commodity. The most widely watched example on MCX is the gold-silver ratio: how many grams (or ounces) of silver it takes to equal the value of one gram (or ounce) of gold.

body.latex: \text{Gold-Silver Ratio} = \frac{\text{Gold price per unit weight}}{\text{Silver price per unit weight}}
body.caption: Both prices must be in the same weight unit (both per gram, or both per troy ounce) for the ratio to mean anything.

body.title: Calculate the ratio
body.prompt: Using illustrative prices, gold is at ₹60,000 per 10 grams (₹6,000/gram) and silver is at ₹90,000 per kg (₹90/gram). What is the gold-silver ratio, rounded to one decimal?
body.explanation: 6,000 ÷ 90 = 66.7. This means it takes about 66.7 grams of silver to equal the value of 1 gram of gold at these illustrative prices.

children.text: Traders watch this ratio against its own recent historical range rather than any fixed 'correct' number, since the range itself shifts over time. If the ratio looks unusually high relative to where it has traded recently, a trader might conclude silver looks cheap relative to gold, and express that view by buying silver futures and selling gold futures (sized so both legs represent roughly similar rupee value), profiting if silver outperforms gold in relative terms, largely independent of whether both metals rise or fall together.

body.text: This is exactly the arbitrageur mindset introduced in Chapter 1: the trade is not a bet on gold or silver's direction, it is a bet on their relationship. Both an inter-commodity spread and a calendar spread share this defining feature, which is why both belong in the same lesson despite trading very different legs.

children.text: A Spread You Understand but Cannot Yet Trade Domestically: The Crack Spread

markDefs.definition: The margin an oil refiner earns from turning crude oil into refined products like petrol and diesel, commonly measured internationally as a spread between crude and refined product futures.

children.text: Globally, refiners and traders watch the

, the refining margin between crude oil and its refined products, as a real-time gauge of refiner profitability. It is a textbook inter-commodity spread. MCX has applied to SEBI in the past to launch petrol and diesel futures, but as of this writing, no such contracts are listed on MCX, so an Indian trader cannot construct a domestic crack spread the way a US trader can with NYMEX crude, gasoline and heating oil contracts. It is still worth understanding conceptually: refining margins are exactly why petrol and diesel prices at an Indian pump do not move in lockstep with crude oil, even though crude is the dominant input cost.

body.title: Calendar spread or inter-commodity spread?
body.scenario: Two traders describe their positions. Trader A has bought the 3-month MCX Natural Gas contract and sold the 1-month MCX Natural Gas contract. Trader B has bought MCX Crude Oil futures and sold MCX Natural Gas futures, betting the two energy commodities' prices will move closer together than they currently are.
body.prompt: Classify each trader's position, and explain what each is fundamentally betting on.
body.modelAnswer: Trader A holds a calendar spread: both legs are the same commodity (natural gas), different contract months, and the bet is purely on how the near-month versus far-month price gap evolves, independent of natural gas's overall price direction. Trader B holds an inter-commodity spread: the legs are two different commodities (crude oil and natural gas), and the bet is on how their prices move relative to each other, independent of whether energy prices broadly rise or fall.

cards.definition: A position built from two related contracts, profiting from the change in the price difference between them rather than the direction of either one.
A spread built from two different contract months of the same commodity.
A spread built across two different but related commodities.
The price of gold divided by the price of silver, in matching weight units, used to gauge the metals' relative valuation.
The refining margin between crude oil and its refined products, traded internationally as an inter-commodity spread; not yet directly tradeable via petrol/diesel futures on an Indian exchange.

points: A spread trade profits from the change in a price relationship between two contracts, not from the absolute direction of either leg.
A calendar spread trades two contract months of the same commodity, directly expressing a view on the cost-of-carry gap covered in Chapter 2.
An inter-commodity spread, like the gold-silver ratio, trades the relationship between two different but related commodities.
Spreads generally carry lower risk, lower potential reward, and sometimes lower margin than an outright position, because the two legs partly offset a broad market move.
Understanding a spread concept, like the crack spread, is useful even when the exact instrument to trade it is not yet available on Indian exchanges.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Spread margin benefits, contract availability and typical historical ranges for ratios like the gold-silver ratio change over time; verify current details with your broker and the exchange before trading.
